blocks.text: The median is the middle value of a dataset once every value has been sorted from smallest to largest. Where the previous lesson's mean is pulled around by every single value, including extreme ones, the median only cares about which value sits in the middle position, which makes it far less sensitive to a handful of unusual numbers. This lesson builds directly on the mean lesson that came before it, reusing the same salary example to make the contrast between the two measures as concrete as possible.

blocks.alt: A dataset sorted and reduced to its middle value, the median
blocks.caption: The median as the middle value of a sorted dataset

blocks.text: 1. What the Median Represents

The median splits an ordered dataset into two equal halves, half of the values fall at or below the median, and half fall at or above it. It answers a different question than the mean does, instead of what value balances the total sum, the median asks what value sits exactly in the middle once everything is lined up in order.

This ordering requirement is the median's defining trait. The mean can be computed straight from a formula without ever sorting anything, but the median has no meaning until the data has been arranged from smallest to largest, since middle position is only defined relative to an order.
This makes the median a positional measure, it cares only about rank order, where a value sits once everything is lined up, not about the actual magnitude of that value or any other.
2. Finding the Median in an Odd Length Dataset

When a dataset has an odd number of values, the median is simply the single value that lands exactly in the middle position after sorting. There is never any ambiguity or averaging required in this case.

code.content:
data = [7, 2, 9, 4, 5]
sorted_data = sorted(data)
print(sorted_data)   # [2, 4, 5, 7, 9]

# 5 values, middle position is index 2 (0-indexed)
median = sorted_data[2]
print(median)   # 5

blocks.text: With five sorted values, the third value has exactly two values below it and two values above it, satisfying the definition of splitting the data into two equal halves.
The middle position for n sorted values can be found directly with the formula (n plus 1) divided by 2, which for 5 values gives position 3, matching the third sorted value exactly.
3. Finding the Median in an Even Length Dataset

When a dataset has an even number of values, there is no single value sitting exactly in the middle, instead there are two values that share the middle position. The median in this case is defined as the average of those two middle values.

code.content:
data = [7, 2, 9, 4, 5, 12]
sorted_data = sorted(data)
print(sorted_data)   # [2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 12]

# 6 values, the two middle positions are index 2 and 3
median = (sorted_data[2] + sorted_data[3]) / 2
print(median)   # 6.0

blocks.text: Notice this median of 6.0 is not a value that appears anywhere in the original dataset, much like the mean can land on a value nothing in the data actually equals. The difference is that the median gets there only by averaging two neighboring middle values, not by weighting every value in the whole dataset.
4. Computing the Median in Code

Both numpy and pandas expose a median function that handles the odd and even length cases automatically, so you rarely need to write the sorting and indexing logic by hand outside of a learning exercise.

code.content:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

odd_data = [7, 2, 9, 4, 5]
print(np.median(odd_data))     # 5.0

even_data = [7, 2, 9, 4, 5, 12]
print(np.median(even_data))    # 6.0

series = pd.Series(even_data)
print(series.median())         # 6.0

blocks.text: These built in functions sort the data internally before locating the middle position, so you can pass in data in any original order and still get the correct median back.
5. Robustness to Outliers

This is where the median earns its reputation as the outlier resistant measure of center. Recall the salary example from the mean lesson: five employees earning close to 45000, plus one executive earning 900000. The mean of that dataset more than quadrupled once the outlier was added, but watch what happens to the median instead.

code.content:
import numpy as np

salaries = [42000, 45000, 47000, 46000, 44000]
print(np.median(salaries))   # 45000.0
print(np.mean(salaries))     # 44800.0

salaries_with_outlier = salaries + [900000]
print(np.median(salaries_with_outlier))   # 45500.0
print(np.mean(salaries_with_outlier))     # 187333.33

blocks.text: Adding the 900000 outlier barely moved the median at all, from 45000 to 45500, while the mean jumped from 44800 all the way to 187333.33. The median only shifted because adding a sixth value changed which two values sit in the middle, it never directly incorporates the outlier's actual magnitude into the calculation the way the mean's sum does.

This resistance comes directly from the rank based nature described in section 1, an extreme value can only ever shift its own rank, it can never drag the middle position toward itself the way it drags the mean.
6. Visualizing the Mean and Median Side by Side

Plotting the mean and median of the same skewed dataset on a single number line makes their different behavior easy to see at a glance. When a dataset has a long tail of large values stretching off to one side, the mean gets dragged toward that tail while the median stays anchored near the bulk of the data.

blocks.alt: The median staying near the cluster of typical values while the mean is pulled toward a single far away outlier
blocks.caption: The mean gets pulled toward the outlier on the right, the median barely moves

blocks.text: Notice the median sits comfortably inside the dense cluster of points on the left, exactly where a typical value falls, while the mean is dragged well to the right by a single distant point, landing in a region with almost no actual data.
7. Properties of the Median

items: The median always lies between the minimum and maximum values of the dataset, just like the mean.
At least half of the data is less than or equal to the median, and at least half is greater than or equal to it, by definition.
The median is unaffected by how far outliers sit from the rest of the data, only their relative rank matters, not their actual magnitude.
Unlike the mean, the median requires the data to be sortable, it has no meaning for data that has no natural order, such as unordered categories.

Adding a constant to every value shifts the median by that same constant, and scaling every value by a positive constant scales the median by that same constant, matching the equivalent mean properties.

blocks.text: The rank based nature of the median explains both its main strength, outlier resistance, and its main limitation, it throws away information about exactly how large or small the non-central values are, since only their order matters.
8. When to Reach for the Median Instead of the Mean

blocks.content: {"headers":["Situation","Prefer mean","Prefer median"],"rows":[["Data has extreme outliers or a long tail","No","Yes"],["Data is roughly symmetric with no outliers","Yes","Either works, similar result"],["You need every value to influence the result","Yes","No"],["Reporting typical income, home prices, or response times","No","Yes"]]}

blocks.text: Income, home prices, and latency measurements are classic examples of right skewed data, a small number of very large values stretch the distribution's tail, which is exactly why government income statistics and real estate listings typically report median figures rather than mean figures.

A quick habit worth building: compare the mean and median of any new dataset side by side, a large gap between them is itself a useful, fast signal that the data is skewed or contains outliers worth investigating further.
9. The Median and Mean Absolute Error

Just as the mean is the value that minimizes total squared distance to a set of points, the median is the value that minimizes total absolute distance to a set of points. This is a direct, non-obvious parallel: mean pairs with squared error, and median pairs with absolute error.

This is exactly why mean absolute error, or MAE, is a popular loss function choice for regression tasks with noisy or outlier heavy data, a model trained to minimize MAE gets pulled toward the median of the target values rather than toward the mean, mirroring the outlier resistance demonstrated earlier in this lesson.

This pairing, mean with squared error and median with absolute error, is a genuinely useful thing to remember when choosing a loss function, the choice of loss quietly determines which central tendency measure the model ends up optimizing toward.
10. Median in Robust Preprocessing

Before feeding numeric features into a machine learning model, it is common to scale them so that no single feature dominates purely because of its raw magnitude. Standard scaling subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, but both of those quantities are themselves distorted by outliers, which can produce a poor scaling when outliers are present.

code.content:
from sklearn.preprocessing import RobustScaler
import numpy as np

data = np.array([[42000], [45000], [47000], [46000], [44000], [900000]])

scaler = RobustScaler()   # uses the median and interquartile range instead of mean and standard deviation
scaled = scaler.fit_transform(data)
print(scaled.ravel())

blocks.text: Scikit-learn's RobustScaler is built specifically around the median rather than the mean, for exactly the same reason the median was introduced in this lesson, it produces a scaling that better reflects the bulk of typical values instead of being skewed by a small number of extreme ones.
11. Median of Grouped or Binned Data

Sometimes raw individual values are not available, only counts within ranges, or bins, such as a histogram of ages grouped into ten year buckets. Estimating a median from this kind of grouped data requires a slightly different technique than sorting a plain list of numbers.
11.1 The Interpolated Median Formula
For grouped data, the median is estimated by finding which bin contains the middle position, then linearly interpolating within that bin based on how far into it the middle position falls.

code.content:
# simplified interpolated median for grouped data
# L: lower boundary of the median bin
# n: total count, cf: cumulative count before the median bin
# f: frequency of the median bin, h: bin width
def interpolated_median(L, n, cf, f, h):
    return L + ((n / 2 - cf) / f) * h

# example: median bin is 30-40, L=30, n=100, cf=42, f=25, h=10
print(interpolated_median(30, 100, 42, 25, 10))   # 33.2

blocks.text: This interpolation is an approximation, since the exact individual values inside each bin are unknown, but it is the standard technique used whenever only aggregated, binned data is available rather than the full raw dataset.
12. Sample Median Versus Population Median

Just as the mean lesson distinguished between a population mean and a sample mean, the same distinction applies to the median. A sample median, computed from a smaller collected subset, is used as an estimate of the true, usually unknown, population median.

The sample median tends to be a noisier estimate than the sample mean for data that is actually free of outliers, since it depends on only one or two central values rather than the entire sample. This tradeoff, more robustness to outliers but sometimes higher variability on clean data, is a central theme running through the comparison between these two measures.
13. Median Absolute Deviation

Just as standard deviation measures spread around the mean, the median absolute deviation, or MAD, measures spread around the median, computed by taking the median of the absolute differences between each value and the overall median. It shares the median own outlier resistance, making it a far more robust spread measure than standard deviation when a dataset contains extreme values.

code.content:
import numpy as np
data = np.array([2, 3, 2, 5, 1, 4, 2, 100])
median_val = np.median(data)
mad = np.median(np.abs(data - median_val))
print(median_val, mad)   # the outlier barely disturbs either number

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: The standard deviation of this same dataset is dramatically inflated by the single value of 100, while the median absolute deviation stays small and representative of how tightly the other seven values actually cluster together, exactly the same outlier resistance the median itself provides for central tendency.

blocks.text: 14. Worked Example

Return to the online store's order sizes from the mean lesson: 2, 3, 2, 5, 1, 4, 2, 45, where the final order was an unusual wholesale purchase. Compute the median of this dataset and compare it to the mean computed previously.

code.content:
import numpy as np

orders = [2, 3, 2, 5, 1, 4, 2, 45]
sorted_orders = sorted(orders)
print(sorted_orders)   # [1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 45]

print(np.median(orders))   # 2.5, average of the two middle values, 2 and 3
print(np.mean(orders))     # 8.0, from the mean lesson

blocks.text: The median of 2.5 items is a far more representative description of a typical order than the mean of 8.0, precisely because the single wholesale order of 45 items barely affects the median, it just becomes one more large value stacked at the end of the sorted list, while it dramatically inflates the mean.
15. Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to sort the data before locating the middle position, which gives a meaningless result if the data is used in its original, unsorted order.
Picking only one of the two middle values in an even length dataset instead of averaging them, producing a value that does not actually split the data into equal halves.
Assuming the median is always close to the mean, when in fact the gap between them is often the clearest early signal that a dataset is skewed or contains outliers.
Trying to compute a median on unordered categorical data, such as a list of colors, where no meaningful middle position exists.
Using the plain median formula on grouped or binned data without applying the interpolation technique, producing a coarse estimate that ignores the internal structure of each bin.

blocks.text: 16. Practice: Compute the Median in Code

Revisit the website visitor data from the mean lesson practice exercise: 120, 135, 128, 142, 130, 138, 125, 133, 129, 140, 131, 3500, 127, 136. Compute the median and compare it against both the plain mean and the mean with the outlier removed, computed previously.

code.content:
import numpy as np

visitors = [120, 135, 128, 142, 130, 138, 125, 133, 129, 140, 131, 3500, 127, 136]

print(np.median(visitors))
print(np.mean(visitors))

without_outlier = [v for v in visitors if v != max(visitors)]
print(np.mean(without_outlier))

blocks.text: Notice that the median lands close to the mean computed with the outlier removed, without you ever having to identify and manually strip out the unusual value yourself, which is exactly the practical convenience that makes the median so useful for messy, real world data.
Key Takeaway

The median absolute deviation from section 13 pairs naturally with the median itself, together they give a complete, outlier resistant description of both center and spread, an alternative to the mean and standard deviation pairing whenever a dataset is heavily skewed or contains extreme values.

The median describes the center of a dataset by rank rather than by magnitude, it is simply the value sitting in the middle once everything is sorted, which makes it highly resistant to outliers that would otherwise distort the mean covered in the previous lesson. The same salary and order examples used throughout both lessons showed the mean swinging wildly while the median barely moved, a direct, concrete illustration of why the median is the preferred measure of center for skewed, real world data.

The median's usefulness extends well beyond simple reporting, it minimizes total absolute error the way the mean minimizes total squared error, it anchors robust feature scaling techniques like RobustScaler, and it is the 50th percentile of a dataset, a connection the next lesson on percentiles builds on directly. Understanding both the mean and the median, and knowing when each one tells a more honest story, is one of the most immediately useful skills in all of statistics.
The mode lesson immediately ahead covers a third, distinct measure of central tendency, one that works even for categorical data where neither the mean nor the median can be computed at all.
